source.title: Wasserstein Distances, Neuronal Entanglement, and Sparsity
source.authors: Shashata Sawmya; Linghao Kong; Ilia Markov; Dan Alistarh; N. Shavit

page_placements.theme: Superposition and interpretability measures change over training
Heavy-tailed activation or weight statistics single out distinct neurons

record.tranche_reason: The paper uses neuronal entanglement and polysemanticity as motivation for a sparsification method and reports results about its own entanglement metrics and method. It does not test semantic responses to unrelated inputs, which the claim versions specify.
record.gate_note: The paper operationalizes entanglement using output-distribution Wasserstein distance (WD) and mapping difficulty (MD), then studies effects on sparsification. These are not tests of whether neurons respond to unrelated semantic inputs or whether those inputs share a feature; the reported results are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The paper treats all neurons as polysemantic by assumption and defines 'entanglement' as an output distribution's Wasserstein distance to a Gaussian, plus its own mapping-difficulty metric. It never checks whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs or concepts, in vision or language models. It does not test superposition, capacity, architecture or measurement dependence either. Its results describe its proxy metrics and its Sparse Expansion sparsification framework, a different construct from any version, so they belong under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also posit that a neuron's robustness to sparsity depends directly on its degree of entanglement. They suspect every neuron is entangled to some degree, Wasserstein neurons most of all.
record.recipe_differences: The study introduces WD/MD measurements and the Sparse Expansion framework; it does not reproduce the original neuron-interpretability methods.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported WD response to sparsification differs between high-WD neurons and low-WD or random neurons; the paper also reports different sparsification effects across neuron-selection criteria and sparsity levels.

fits_no_version.finding: A small set of FFN neurons in Pythia-1.4B, Llama-2-7B and Llama-3-8B have highly non-Gaussian output distributions (high WD to a Gaussian). WD correlates strongly with mapping difficulty.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Transformer FFN layers contain a minority of neurons with strongly non-Gaussian outputs that map similar inputs to dissimilar outputs; the paper labels this 'entanglement'.

fits_no_version.finding: Sparsifying high-WD neurons harms Llama-3-8B more than sparsifying random or other selected neurons. Sparsification makes their outputs more Gaussian. Input-clustered sparse experts reduce their WD and MD most.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: High-WD 'entangled' neurons are disproportionately sensitive to weight sparsification.

fits_no_version.finding: High-WD neurons emerge within about 10-20B tokens of Pythia training, without larger weight changes than other neurons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Non-Gaussian neuron output distributions arise early in training.

record.problems: The paper's entanglement measures are indirect distributional and input-output metrics, not semantic feature explanations. Several comparisons are described through figures without exact values in the text; uncertainty is not stated for many reported outcomes.
record.rows_left_out: Left out broader pruning-performance comparisons in Figure 9 and Tables A1–A5, cluster-count performance sweeps, and inference-latency results because they evaluate the sparsification method rather than neuron polysemanticity or the reported WD/MD entanglement measures.

untested.parts: No count of neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts. WD outliers by layer (Figure A1) are a distribution-shape proxy, not semantic polysemanticity.
Superposition is invoked as motivation only. Feature count vs neuron capacity is not manipulated against a polysemanticity measure.
Training-checkpoint WD trajectories are not a test of polysemanticity arising without capacity pressure.
Activation function, architecture and regularization are not compared.
No neuron's inputs are interpreted semantically.
No comparison of activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods for polysemanticity judgments.

record.verdict_notes: The study uses the term 'polysemantic' throughout but redefines it via distribution shape. No semantic test is performed, so no verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: No image classifiers or vision neurons are studied.
No unrelated tokens or contexts are identified or counted, and no layer-wise prevalence of semantic polysemanticity is measured.
The study discusses superposition and varies input clustering, but does not test whether excess feature capacity causes semantic polysemanticity.
The study does not test whether polysemantic neurons arise without capacity pressure from initialization, regularization, or training noise.
No comparison of activation functions, architectures, or regularization as causes of changes in semantic polysemanticity is reported.
The study does not interpret the semantic features of the neurons or determine whether apparently mixed responses share a coherent feature.
The study introduces WD and MD but does not compare semantic polysemanticity judgments across activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods.

relation.reason: The paper refers to all neurons as polysemantic by assumption and builds a metric and a pruning framework on that, with no semantic test.

tranche.reason: The paper takes polysemanticity as a premise, builds WD/MD metrics and Sparse Expansion, and reports results on those. It never tests whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs or concepts, so its findings fit no version.

source_check.notes: Rows are accurate. Main text and appendix caption disagree on the Figure A2a/A2b labels. WD measures distribution shape and MD measures output separation, so neither is a semantic polysemanticity measure. The MD-WD link and the training-dynamics results come from one layer of Pythia-1.4B.

statements.correction: Main text: Wasserstein neurons arise within 10-20B tokens. Appendix caption: within 5,000 steps (~10B tokens), then WD levels off. High-WD (top 3%) neurons show no more relative L2 weight change than the average or bottom-3% WD neurons. Pythia-1.4B, up projection of the second FFN block, 17 checkpoints.
statements.problem: Right. Main text gives 10-20B tokens; the appendix caption gives about 10B tokens (5,000 steps). The weight-change claim matches both the main text and the caption. The result covers one layer of Pythia-1.4B.

statements.correction: A small group of neurons with highly non-Gaussian outputs (high WD) is reported in all FFNs of Pythia-1.4B, Llama-2-7B and Llama-3-8B. The MD-WD correlation is shown only for Pythia-1.4B, up projection of the second FFN block, on Wikitext-2 inputs (Figure 2e, no coefficient). The paper calls Wasserstein neurons 'particularly entangled'.
statements.problem: The high-WD part is right for all three models. But the sentence implies the WD-MD correlation holds across them, and it is shown only for one layer of Pythia-1.4B ('highly correlated', no coefficient given).
